title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 9: Invalid Plea Bargain
keywords: the offended party did not consent
the Republic... is the offended party
retired Maj. Gen. Carlos F. Garcia
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's January 30, 2011 Inquirer column arguing that the plea-bargaining documents that released retired Maj. Gen. Carlos Garcia from detention are 'invalid' -- the undated Plea Bargaining Agreement (PBA) with the Ombudsman, the May 4, 2010 Sandiganbayan (SBN) resolution, and the December 16, 2010 SBN resolution granting bail

His first ground: the PBA lacked the consent of the 'offended party.' Under Rule 116 of the Rules of Court a guilty plea to a lesser offense needs the consent of both the prosecutor and the offended party -- and in plunder the offended party is 'the Republic' (represented by the OSG), which was 'not mentioned at all' and never consented, especially crucial since Garcia ceded only ~P135 million against a P303-million claim

His second ground: the SBN never evaluated the evidence. A plea to a lesser crime must come 'at arraignment' or 'before trial,' yet Garcia's came after the prosecution had rested; the narrow exception (allowed only when the prosecution lacks sufficient evidence) requires a finding on 'the weight of the evidence' (People v. Villarama), which the May 4 resolution lacked -- though the SBN had earlier denied bail because the evidence was 'strong'

His conclusion that the December 16 bail-and-release order, resting on the invalid May 4 resolution, is likewise irregular (as is extending the deal's benefits to Garcia's wife and sons abroad) -- but 'all is not lost,' since the SBN can still recall its resolutions and order Garcia's re-confinement
sub_topics: The three challenged documents: the undated 'Plea Bargaining Agreement' (PBA) between the Office of the Ombudsman and Garcia; the May 4, 2010 SBN resolution ordering Garcia to convey listed properties before the PBA could be approved; and the December 16, 2010 SBN resolution granting bail and releasing him

The background: in 2005 the Ombudsman charged Garcia, his wife Clarita and three sons (plus three 'Does') with the non-bailable crime of plunder and, separately, money laundering; in the PBA Garcia offered to plead guilty to the 'lesser offenses' of indirect bribery and facilitating money laundering if plunder and money laundering were withdrawn, ceding properties worth about P135 million against the Information's P303-million plunder claim

The governing rule: Section 2 of Rule 116 lets an accused, 'with the consent of the offended party and the prosecutor,' plead guilty to a lesser offense 'necessarily included' in the charge, 'at arraignment' or, at the latest, 'before trial'

First defect -- no consent by the Republic: the prosecutors consented, 'but clearly also, the offended party did not'; the offended party is the entity 'directly damaged' (in plunder, 'the Republic'), as the Information itself admits ('to the damage of the Filipino people and the Republic'), and the Republic is represented by the OSG, not the prosecutors -- consent being 'especially essential' because P135 million is far less than the P303-million claim

Second defect -- no evaluation of evidence: the plea must come at arraignment or before trial (to 'save government resources and time' and unclog dockets), but Garcia's came after the prosecution rested; the exception allowing a late plea applies 'only when the prosecution does not have sufficient evidence,' which requires a finding on 'the weight of the evidence in hand' (People v. Villarama, 1992) -- a finding the May 4 resolution never made

The contradiction: 'worse,' the SBN had on January 7, 2010 denied Garcia bail precisely because it found the prosecution's evidence 'strong' -- undercutting any claim that the evidence was insufficient

Third defect -- a derivative order: the December 16, 2010 bail-and-release resolution is 'likewise irregular' because it rests on the invalid May 4 resolution; moreover, only Garcia signed the PBA, yet its benefits were extended to his wife and sons 'in the United States, outside the jurisdiction of our courts'
The remedy: 'all is not lost,' since the SBN 'can still correct these lapses... by recalling its two Resolutions and ordering the re-confinement of the accused'

stances.claim: The Garcia plea bargain is invalid for lack of the offended party's consent: Rule 116 requires the consent of both prosecutor and offended party, and in plunder the offended party is 'the Republic' (represented by the OSG, not the prosecutors), which was never even mentioned -- a defect made graver because P135 million is far less than the P303-million claim.
stances.rhetorical_move: element-by-element invalidation: applying the rule's text to show a missing prerequisite
stances.confidence: asserted as legal opinion ('in my humble view')

stances.claim: The plea is also invalid because the Sandiganbayan never evaluated the evidence: a late plea (after the prosecution rests) is allowed only when the evidence is insufficient and requires a finding on 'the weight of the evidence' (People v. Villarama) -- which the May 4 resolution lacked, and which contradicts the court's own earlier finding that the evidence was 'strong.'
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-defect plus contradiction: pairing the missing finding with the court's prior bail denial

stances.claim: The release order is therefore irregular and the benefits cannot extend to absent co-accused -- but 'all is not lost,' because the Sandiganbayan can recall its resolutions and order Garcia's re-confinement.
stances.rhetorical_move: consequence-and-cure: drawing the downstream defect, then offering a corrective path

notable_anecdotes: P135M for P303M: CJP underscores that Garcia offered to cede only about P135 million against the Information's P303-million plunder claim -- making the Republic's (absent) consent all the more essential.

Who is the offended party?: he explains by analogy -- in rape the violated person, in murder the heirs, in theft the owner -- that in plunder it is 'the Republic,' represented by the OSG, not the prosecutors.
The court's own contradiction: he notes the Sandiganbayan had denied bail on January 7, 2010 because the evidence was 'strong,' then accepted a plea premised on insufficiency.
Benefits for the absent: he flags that only Garcia signed, yet the deal's benefits reached his wife and sons 'in the United States, outside the jurisdiction of our courts.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's January 30, 2011 Inquirer column, argues that the documents that freed retired Maj. Gen. Carlos Garcia are 'in my humble view, invalid' -- the undated Plea Bargaining Agreement (PBA) with the Ombudsman, the May 4, 2010 Sandiganbayan (SBN) resolution, and the December 16, 2010 resolution granting bail. The background: in 2005 the Ombudsman charged Garcia, his wife and three sons with non-bailable plunder and, separately, money laundering; in the PBA Garcia offered to plead guilty to the lesser offenses of indirect bribery and facilitating money laundering -- ceding properties worth about P135 million against the Information's P303-million claim -- if the graver charges were dropped. CJP's first ground: Rule 116 lets an accused plead to a lesser offense only 'with the consent of the offended party and the prosecutor,' and while the prosecutors consented, the offended party did not -- indeed was 'not mentioned at all.' In plunder, he explains, the offended party is 'the Republic' (acknowledged in the Information itself and represented by the OSG, not the prosecutors), whose consent was 'especially essential' given the P135-million-for-P303-million gap. His second ground: a plea to a lesser crime must come 'at arraignment' or 'before trial,' yet Garcia's came after the prosecution had rested; the narrow exception applies 'only when the prosecution does not have sufficient evidence' and requires a finding on 'the weight of the evidence' (People v. Villarama, 1992) -- a finding the May 4 resolution never made, and one contradicted by the SBN's own January 7, 2010 denial of bail because the evidence was 'strong.' The December 16 bail-and-release order, resting on the invalid May 4 resolution, is therefore 'likewise irregular,' and CJP flags that only Garcia signed even as the deal's benefits reached his wife and sons 'in the United States, outside the jurisdiction of our courts.' Still, 'all is not lost': the Sandiganbayan 'can still correct these lapses... by recalling its two Resolutions and ordering the re-confinement of the accused.'
